variants.markdown:
**English draft for R5 review.**

Think of a piggy bank. Coins **go in** when you get pocket money or a gift from Nani. Coins **come out** when you buy a pencil or a samosa.

Money coming in is called **income**. Money going out is called **spending**. If more goes out than comes in, the piggy bank gets empty!

So before you buy something, peek inside: how much came in, and how much is left?

Gullak uses virtual play money only.

questions.prompt: Nani gives you ₹50 on your birthday. Is that money coming in or going out?
questions.explanation: A gift adds money to your piggy bank, so it is coming in.

questions.prompt: You buy a ₹10 eraser. What happens to your money?
questions.explanation: Buying something means money goes out.

questions.prompt: What happens if more money goes out than comes in?
questions.explanation: Spending more than you get leaves nothing behind.

variants.markdown:
**English draft for R5 review.**

Every household runs on **cash flow**: money in minus money out over a period.

**Inflows** can be active income (a salary, a part-time job, tuition fees you earn), passive income (interest, rent) or one-off receipts (gifts, a scholarship). **Outflows** split into **fixed** costs that barely change month to month (rent, school fees, an EMI) and **variable** costs that do (food, travel, fun).

If inflows are greater than outflows, you have a **surplus** you can save or invest. If outflows are greater, you run a **deficit**, which is covered by savings or borrowing. Neither can last forever: a long deficit drains savings and builds debt.

A useful habit is to look at the **net** figure every month, not just the income. A high earner with higher spending is worse off than a modest earner with a steady surplus.

Gullak uses virtual play money only.

questions.prompt: Kiran earns ₹18,000 a month from a part-time job and spends ₹15,500. What is the monthly cash flow?
questions.explanation: ₹18,000 in minus ₹15,500 out leaves a ₹2,500 surplus.

questions.prompt: Which of these is usually a fixed cost?
questions.explanation: Rent stays the same each month; the others change with choices.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of passive income?
questions.explanation: Interest arrives without extra work each month; the others pay for work or are one-offs.

questions.prompt: What happens if a household runs a deficit for many months?

options.text: Nothing, as long as income is high

questions.explanation: A deficit has to be paid from savings or borrowing, so one or both suffer.
